# Gaggia Classic Notes

## Setup

I bought the machine second-hand from a man who had moved on to something with a rotary pump, so the price was fair and the body was sound apart from a scuffed drip tray. The first job was the over-pressure valve, because a gauge on a blind filter told me the group was running high. I replaced the OPV spring so the group runs 9.5 bar, and it took an afternoon of trial and error, swapping springs and taking readings until the needle settled where I wanted it. The valve body on this model is brass, which takes a spring change without complaint and does not corrode the way the older alloy ones do. There is a PID on the boiler now, driven by a solid state relay with a thermocouple bolted to the side of the boiler, and the temperature holds far steadier than it ever did on the original thermostat. I can watch the reading climb after a flush and pull the shot when it recovers. The pump is a 48 W vibration pump, still the original unit, noisy but reliable. I changed the shower screen and gasket while the machine was open, since both were caked with old grounds and the gasket had gone hard. Bean age matters more than any of the hardware, so I seal the bag and use it between about five and twenty days off roast, and I weigh beans rather than guessing at the scoop.

## Cleaning

I rinse the drip tray every evening and dry it, because the oils go sticky overnight and are far harder to shift the next morning. The group gasket gets wiped with a damp cloth after the last shot of the day, running the cloth around the rim where the basket seats, which keeps the rubber supple and stops it cracking. The basket comes out and is brushed clean with a stiff nylon brush under the tap, then left to dry on the rack. Once a week I take the shower screen off and scrub it under hot water with the same brush, working the holes clear of fines. The steam wand gets a wipe straight after milk, before the residue sets, and the tip is left in a jug of water for a minute. The reservoir is rinsed and refilled with filtered water, and the casing is wiped down with a barely damp cloth. I dry everything before it goes back together so nothing corrodes at the seams.

## Troubleshooting

Sour shots are the complaint I meet most often, and nine times out of ten they mean the grind is too coarse or the water is not hot enough. When a shot gushes through in fifteen seconds and the crema is thin and blond, I leave the beans alone and tighten the grind one notch, then dry the basket with a cloth before dosing, because a wet basket clumps the grounds at the bottom. Channelling shows up under the naked portafilter as jets of liquid spitting sideways while the centre of the puck stays dry, and the cure is the same grind adjustment plus a quicker, flatter tamp. If the grind is already fine and the shot still gushes, I raise the boiler setpoint to 96 C and give the machine ten minutes to settle before pulling again. That one change fixes most of what I used to blame on the beans. A basket that sticks to the gasket points at a worn gasket rather than the grind. When the pump labours and the flow stutters, the reservoir is usually low or the intake is airlocked. I keep a small notebook of grind setting, time and yield for each bag, because the grinder drifts a touch as it warms and the note saves me chasing the same setting twice. If the group still feels cool to the touch after a long warm up, the thermocouple has probably worked loose from the boiler, and that is a five minute job to nip back up with a spanner.

## Notes

I pull my shots at 27 s for 34 g, weighing the cup on the scale and cutting the pump by time rather than by eye. That ratio suits most medium roasts and gives me a starting point whenever a new bag arrives. Beans sit best between 7 and 14 days off roast, so I write the roast date on the bag and try not to open it early. Anything older than three weeks tastes flat and thin no matter how I adjust the grind. I keep a spare gasket and a spare shower screen in the drawer, since both are cheap and both fail at the worst possible moment. The drip tray and the group get most of my attention, and the rest of the machine is happy as long as the water stays filtered and the beans stay fresh.
